message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear).
• Landlords must provide a written itemized list of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in inspection report, and any receipts for repairs.
• Request a written receipt for the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a habitable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural safety).
• If the landlord fails to maintain habitability, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or terminate the lease. | • Document problems with photos and written notices.
• Give the landlord a reasonable time to fix issues before taking further action. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• No statutory cap on rent increases. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses.
• Ask for a written notice of any increase. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a valid reason (e.g., non‑payment, violation of lease) and follow the notice requirements. | • Keep copies of all notices.
• If you’re being evicted, you have the right to a hearing before the court. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an unlawful detainer action. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you receive an eviction notice, you can file a counter‑claim or request a hearing. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlords must give reasonable notice (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • Report any discriminatory actions to the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, provided you follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable time). | • Keep receipts and document the repair. | | **Right to a Written Lease** | • While not required by Texas law, having a written lease protects both parties. | • Always sign a lease and keep a copy. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • The lease may restrict subletting; if allowed, you must follow the lease terms. | • Get written permission if required. | | **Landlord’s Right to Inspect** | • Landlords can inspect the unit with proper notice, but cannot do so for harassment or discrimination. | • Know your rights to privacy. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand rent amount, due dates, security deposit limits, pet policies, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help protect you in disputes. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month termination, 3‑day notice for non‑payment, etc. 4. **Respond Promptly** – Ignoring notices can lead to eviction. 5. **Seek Legal Help if Needed** – Tenant‑rights groups, legal aid clinics, or a private attorney can assist. ### Resources - **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** – Provides tenant‑rights guides. - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – Handles discrimination complaints. - **Legal Aid of North Texas** – Offers free or low‑cost legal assistance. - **Texas Eviction Law** – Online resources explaining the eviction process. --- If you have a specific situation (e.g., a notice you received, a repair issue, or a dispute over rent), let me know and I can give more tailored guidance.
